facts.text: The Living Planet Report 2026, produced by WWF and the Zoological Society of London, was published in October 2026.
The 2026 Living Planet Index covers 35,803 monitored populations of 5,790 vertebrate species: mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish.
Between 1970 and 2022 the monitored wildlife populations shrank by 73% on average, according to the index.
In the index, a population means one species living in one geographical area.
The index tracks the average change in the size of populations relative to 1970 (1970 = 1); it is not a count of individual animals lost.
The index tells us nothing about how many species have gone extinct or how many populations have been lost.
The index averages proportional changes (a geometric mean), so a small population's rise or fall can weigh as much as that of a much larger one.
One black rhino population in Tanzania fell from 3,795 animals in 1980 to 160 in 2017, while one in Botswana grew from 30 to 50.
Taken together, the two rhino populations lost 3,615 animals, or 95% of the starting total, but the index method gives an average decline of about 74%.
Around half of the populations studied were stable or increasing; the large average decline comes from the fact that declines tend to be bigger than increases.
By habitat, freshwater populations fell by 85% on average between 1970 and 2022, land populations by 69% and marine populations by 59%.
By region, the steepest average decline from 1970 to 2022 was in Latin America and the Caribbean (95%), followed by Africa (80%).
The smaller regional declines were in North America (28%) and Europe and Central Asia (23%) between 1970 and 2022.
Europe and Central Asia's index rose above its 1970 level in the 1980s and 1990s before falling below it.
In October 2025 the IUCN Red List moved the green sea turtle from Endangered to Least Concern.
The global green turtle population has grown by about 28% since the 1970s.

The green turtle's recovery followed decades of protecting nesting females and their eggs on beaches, local efforts to reduce the taking of turtles and eggs, limits on trade, and devices that keep turtles out of fishing gear.
Green turtles are still far below their numbers before European colonisation, and climate change is affecting some nesting beaches.

The index is a geometric mean: the regional value for a year is the average population size compared with 1970, so a value of 19.8 (1970 = 100) means populations were on average about one-fifth of their 1970 size.
